title: Preferring clear instructions to piling up constraints

videos.script: Every rule in a long prompt fixed one bad answer, once. Put thirteen of them together and you have a pile. {{title}} Eight of these rules only say what not to do. Two of them shout. And two contradict each other for a question about money, which the linter cannot see. {{pile}} The other prompt explains the job instead. Each category is described by who answers it, and urgency is about harm, not tone. It is longer, and the linter finds nothing. {{guide}} Then you measure. Seventy messages, both prompts. The guide passes four more, and the sign test cannot tell that from chance. {{measure}} Underneath the totals, the two prompts lean opposite ways. The rules push urgency down; the guide pushes it up. And on the one question the guide was written to settle, the rules got it right. {{limit}} What a reason does give is a reader who can handle a case nobody listed, and a maintainer who knows which rule may go. Whether the model uses it is something you measure. {{close}}
